quote: Thiamine before glucose, every time.

basis: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020) and standard emergency-medicine teaching (e.g., Tintinalli): do not withhold or delay glucose for thiamine in hypoglycemia; give thiamine promptly alongside repletion.

quote: Give **parenteral thiamine** to any patient with heavy alcohol use and suspected or possible Wernicke encephalopathy, and always **before** IV dextrose — a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke [6].
problem: Two problems in one instruction. First, the question's own mnemonic is "banana bag done right," but the text never signals that treatment dosing for suspected Wernicke is roughly an order of magnitude above the prophylactic thiamine in a routine bag, and must be given for several days — under-dosing is the commonest reason a Wernicke that was "treated" still progresses to Korsakoff, and this case lists Wernicke as differential #2 and tells the learner to treat empirically. Second, "always before IV dextrose" is stated as an absolute; in symptomatic hypoglycaemia glucose must not be withheld while thiamine is located. Both belong here because Q6 is the orders question.
replacement: Give **parenteral (IV or IM) thiamine** to any patient with heavy alcohol use, and give **high-dose parenteral thiamine, continued over several days** — substantially more than the thiamine in a routine "banana bag" — whenever Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected; under-dosing is the commonest reason a treated Wernicke still progresses to Korsakoff. Give thiamine **before or together with** IV dextrose, because a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke [6] — but **never delay dextrose in symptomatic hypoglycemia** to hunt for thiamine; give the glucose and give the thiamine with it.
basis: EFNS guideline on Wernicke encephalopathy and Royal College of Physicians guidance: therapeutic parenteral thiamine for suspected Wernicke is far higher and longer than prophylactic dosing; the page's own reference [6] notes guidelines vary widely on dose and duration. No dose literal named here, consistent with the page's stated no-dosing policy — the point is that the learner must not assume the routine bag is a treatment dose.

quote: Before discharge, offer **AUD pharmacotherapy** — **oral naltrexone 50 mg/d** and **acamprosate** are first-line with the strongest evidence (number needed to treat ~11–18 to prevent one person returning to any drinking), alongside psychosocial treatment [9].
problem: Four bullets earlier the same question uses this patient's AST:ALT ratio and platelet count to infer liver disease and choose lorazepam over chlordiazepoxide — then recommends naltrexone in the same patient with no hepatic caveat at all. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is avoided in acute hepatitis or decompensated liver disease (LFTs checked, decision individualised in compensated cirrhosis), and is contraindicated in anyone taking or likely to need opioids — relevant in a man facing operative fracture fixation in two days. Acamprosate, the obvious alternative here, is renally cleared and must be reduced or avoided in significant renal impairment. As written the learner takes away "offer naltrexone," in exactly the patient the page has just built to make organ-matching the point.
replacement: Before discharge, offer **AUD pharmacotherapy** — **oral naltrexone 50 mg/d** and **acamprosate** are first-line with the strongest evidence (number needed to treat ~11–18 to prevent one person returning to any drinking), alongside psychosocial treatment [9]. Match the agent to the organ and to the plan: naltrexone is hepatically metabolized and is avoided in acute hepatitis or decompensated liver disease, and is contraindicated in anyone on or likely to need opioids — note his operative fixation in two days; acamprosate is renally cleared and is dose-reduced or avoided in significant renal impairment. In *this* patient, whose transaminase ratio and platelet count already pointed to liver disease, check the LFTs, plan around the peri-operative analgesia, and consider acamprosate.
basis: FDA labelling for naltrexone (boxed hepatotoxicity warning removed 2013; still contraindicated in acute hepatitis/hepatic failure and in current opioid use) and for acamprosate (renal dose adjustment, contraindicated CrCl <30); ASAM/VA-DoD AUD pharmacotherapy guidance; McPheeters 2023 (the page's ref [9]) for the NNT figures, which are correctly stated.

quote: Office-based prescribing; ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it comparatively safe. **Must be started in withdrawal** or it precipitates withdrawal.
problem: True, but framed as a sufficient rule, and this is a fentanyl case. Because illicitly manufactured fentanyl is lipophilic and accumulates in tissue, precipitated withdrawal still occurs in a meaningful minority of inductions performed at an adequate withdrawal score — which is why low-dose ("micro") and high-dose induction strategies exist, and is the central subject of the page's own reference [3]. A student taught the timing rule as the whole answer will read a precipitated withdrawal as the patient having used again, and will not know that induction in this population is a decision to make with addiction medicine rather than a threshold to clear.
replacement: Office-based prescribing; ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it comparatively safe. **Started only once the patient is in objective withdrawal** — given earlier, its high receptor affinity displaces the full agonist and precipitates withdrawal. With illicitly manufactured fentanyl that rule is necessary but no longer sufficient: fentanyl accumulates in tissue, so precipitated withdrawal still occurs in a minority of inductions done at an adequate withdrawal score, which is why low-dose and high-dose induction strategies exist and why induction here is planned with addiction medicine rather than run off a threshold [3].
basis: Englander 2024, JAMA Intern Med — "Caring for hospitalized adults with opioid use disorder in the era of fentanyl" (the page's ref [3]); ASAM/CMAJ 2024 OUD guideline discussion of alternative buprenorphine initiation strategies in fentanyl exposure.

quote: 3. **Anoxic brain injury** — he was found unresponsive for an unknown period. Persistent confusion, focal deficits, or failure to return to baseline demands imaging and a broader workup, not reassurance.
problem: The differential draws the right lesson from an unwitnessed down-time for the brain and then stops. The other standard consequences of lying immobile on a hard surface — rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia and pigment-induced AKI, and positional compartment syndrome or pressure necrosis in a dependent limb — appear nowhere in the ranked differential, the summary differential, or the whole-patient workup ladder, and no CK is drawn ("CBC and chemistries unremarkable" does not include CK). A missed compartment syndrome costs a limb and a missed rhabdomyolysis costs kidneys, in a patient the page is otherwise about to discharge with a naloxone kit.
replacement: 3. **Consequences of the down-time itself** — he was found unresponsive for an unknown period. **Anoxic brain injury:** persistent confusion, focal deficits, or failure to return to baseline demands imaging and a broader workup, not reassurance. **Rhabdomyolysis:** send a CK with potassium and creatinine and look for pigmented urine — prolonged immobility on a hard surface is the classic mechanism. **Positional compartment syndrome or pressure necrosis:** examine the dependent limb for a tense, disproportionately painful compartment — pain out of proportion with a palpable pulse is still compartment syndrome.
basis: Standard emergency and toxicology practice for the found-down patient; rhabdomyolysis and positional compartment syndrome are recognised complications of prolonged opioid-related immobility and are not detectable on the CBC/chemistry panel the stem reports.

quote: Counsel that **antidepressants take 4–6 weeks at an adequate dose** to show full effect, and that a partial response by 2–4 weeks predicts later response.
problem: This sets full effect at 4–6 weeks; Q3 then defines an adequate trial as "≥6–8 weeks"; and the management ladder tells the learner to "Reassess at 4–6 weeks" and branch straight to switch or augment. Those cannot all govern, and the one the learner acts on — reassess and change at 4–6 weeks — produces precisely the error the facilitator notes say to correct ("declaring a drug 'failed' before 6 weeks/adequate dose"). The case compounds it by labelling a PHQ-9 fall of 16 to 13 — three points, below the roughly five-point minimal clinically important difference — a "partial response," which then routes the learner down the optimise/augment arm on the strength of a change that is within measurement noise.
replacement: Counsel that **antidepressants usually need 4–8 weeks at an adequate dose** for full effect — some improvement is often visible by 2–4 weeks, and the absence of *any* improvement by 4 weeks predicts a low chance of later response — but do not call a trial adequate, or declare it failed, before **6–8 weeks at an adequate dose**. Remember too that the PHQ-9 moves in ~5-point steps to be clinically meaningful: a 16 to 13 change is minimal response, not a partial response.
basis: APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorder (reassess at 4–8 weeks; monitor at 2–4 week intervals); STAR*D, in which remissions continued to accrue out to 8–12 weeks; established PHQ-9 minimal clinically important difference of about 5 points.

quote: Distinguish the three: optimize = push the same drug up; switch = replace it; augment = add a second agent to the first.
problem: "Replace it" is the operative definition on a page whose whole subject is switching, and it carries no mention of how. Abruptly stopping an SSRI or SNRI — paroxetine and venlafaxine worst — produces a discontinuation syndrome of dizziness, electric-shock sensations, flu-like symptoms, irritability and insomnia that is routinely misread as relapse or as an adverse effect of the new drug, and leads either to the switch being abandoned or the old drug being restarted. Cross-tapering is the standard technique. A switch involving an MAOI additionally needs a formal washout to avoid serotonin syndrome.
replacement: Distinguish the three: optimize = push the same drug up; switch = replace it, and in almost all cases by **cross-tapering** rather than stopping abruptly — abrupt cessation of an SSRI or SNRI (paroxetine and venlafaxine are the worst offenders) causes a discontinuation syndrome of dizziness, electric-shock sensations, flu-like symptoms and irritability that is routinely mistaken for relapse, and any switch to or from an MAOI needs a formal washout to avoid serotonin syndrome; augment = add a second agent to the first.
basis: APA MDD guideline and standard psychopharmacology practice on cross-tapering and antidepressant discontinuation syndrome; MAOI washout intervals (drug-dependent, longest for fluoxetine) to avoid serotonin syndrome.

quote: Recognizing a manic episode, screening for mixed features and secondary mania, and choosing first-line acute treatment.

quote: Favor **discharge with a robust safety plan and rapid follow-up** when ideation is passive/low-intent, the patient can collaborate on and commit to a plan, means access can be reduced, and reliable supports and timely outpatient follow-up exist.
problem: Two phrases undo work the page does elsewhere. "Commit to a plan" reimports the logic of the no-suicide contract that Q4 and Q5 have just discarded — a patient's promise is not evidence of safety, and making it a discharge criterion is how the contract survives under a new name. "Means access **can be** reduced" is conditional: it licenses discharge on the theory that means could be secured rather than on confirmation that a named person has secured them. Together they let an ED discharge rest on a promise plus an intention, on the one page whose stated purpose is to teach that risk labels do not predict who acts.
replacement: Favor **discharge with a robust safety plan and rapid follow-up** when ideation is passive and of low intent, the patient can **engage collaboratively** in building the plan (their ability to work on it with you is the signal — a promise to stay safe is not, which is exactly why the no-harm contract was abandoned), means access **has actually been reduced** (a named person has secured or removed the means by an agreed time, and you have documented who and when), and reliable supports plus a confirmed, timely outpatient appointment are in place.
basis: VA/DoD suicide risk CPG on safety planning and means restriction as enacted rather than intended steps; Stanley & Brown Safety Planning Intervention, in which collaborative engagement — not a commitment or contract — is the active element; the page's own Q4/Q5 rejection of the no-suicide contract.

quote: 7. **Treat the underlying disorder** (start/optimize depression treatment; address alcohol use).
problem: The patient is 19 with active ideation and escalating alcohol use, and this is the step at which an antidepressant gets started. Nothing on the page mentions that starting an antidepressant under age 25 carries the FDA boxed warning for treatment-emergent suicidal ideation and behaviour, or that this obliges explicit counselling of the patient and, with consent, a support person about emergent agitation, akathisia, insomnia or worsening ideation, plus close contact through the first weeks — the same weeks in which the drug has not yet worked. A student following this step as written starts an SSRI and books routine follow-up.
replacement: 7. **Treat the underlying disorder** (start/optimize depression treatment; address alcohol use). If an antidepressant is started, note that this patient is under 25: counsel them, and with consent a support person, that emergent agitation, akathisia, insomnia, or worsening suicidal thoughts in the first weeks must be reported the same day, and arrange close contact across that window — the interval before the drug works is also the interval of greatest concern. Means reduction and treating the alcohol use are part of this plan, not separate from it.
basis: FDA class boxed warning for antidepressants (increased risk of suicidal thinking and behaviour in patients aged under 25) and the associated monitoring/counselling expectation; APA MDD guideline on close early follow-up in patients with suicidal ideation.

quote: | Delirium prevention | Multicomponent non-pharmacological | 53% reduction in incident delirium | Meta-analysis of 14 studies |
problem: This row typifies the page-wide pattern: ~13 summary-table rows and roughly two dozen prose statistics pair an effect size with a study design ('Meta-analysis of 14 studies', 'RCT (n=200)', 'Cochrane review (33 RCTs)') but no study identity, so a learner cannot get from any number to a paper even though the page ends in a full DOI bibliography — and the evidence-annotation gate cannot catch a wrong one because it only verifies claims somebody annotated. replacement: | Delirium prevention | Multicomponent non-pharmacological | 53% reduction in incident delirium | Hshieh 2015 meta-analysis of 14 studies (JAMA Intern Med) |

Site policy already requires claim-level traceability (evidence_annotations sourceSpan gate).

quote: produced a **60% reduction in post-discharge suicide attempts** (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20–0.80; NNT = 7)
problem: OR 0.40 is a 60% reduction in the odds of an attempt, not in attempts; with the outcome common enough to give NNT = 7, the implied relative risk reduction is roughly 50%, so the sentence overstates the flagship psychotherapy result. The TL;DR ('reduces post-discharge attempts 60% (NNT 7)') and the summary-table row ('60% reduction in attempts (NNT=7)') repeat the gloss, and learners will quote it to families as '60% fewer attempts'.
replacement: produced a **60% reduction in the odds of a post-discharge suicide attempt** (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20–0.80; NNT = 7)
basis: Odds ratios only approximate risk ratios when the outcome is rare; an NNT of 7 means it is not rare here (baseline risk ~25–30%, at which OR 0.40 corresponds to RR ~0.5). Diefenbach et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2024 reported the effect as an odds ratio.

quote: Outpatient sufficient, Medical workup before treatment, and Lucid interval = reassurance all miss the emergency framing.
problem: The rationale dismisses the medical-workup distractor wholesale without stating that the workup still happens — concurrently. The stem describes acute confusion with a fluctuating course 9 days postpartum, a phenotype where eclampsia/PRES, thyroid disease, infection, and autoimmune encephalitis are on the differential; the distractor is wrong only in its sequencing ('before any psychiatric treatment'), not in the need for the workup. A learner could conclude no organic evaluation is needed in postpartum psychosis, which also contradicts the library's own psychosis items (qb_psy_001, qb_psy_003) teaching exclusion of secondary causes; qb_otherdx_003's rationale ('Medical cause only') repeats the same pattern in softer form.

Medical workup before treatment is wrong only in its sequencing: delirium, eclampsia, thyroid disease, infection, and autoimmune encephalitis are excluded concurrently with emergency psychiatric admission — the organic workup proceeds in parallel and must never delay hospitalization or treatment.

The learner therefore never gets the one explanation this item needs: why bulimia nervosa rather than purging disorder (the presence of recurrent, objectively large binge episodes). quote: Approach calmly, introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter, or is there something I can get you?'
problem: The keyed option — the graded model behavior — has a lone medical student engage a pacing, loud, hand-waving patient without telling any staff member, and offers to move him 'somewhere quieter' (a more isolated space). The bank's own qb_saf_011 keys the opposite for a near-identical scenario ('Signal a nearby staff member that you are approaching... stay near your exit and never block the patient's'). A learner rehearsing to this key practices solo engagement without backup and relocation of an agitated patient away from observation; the two items also leave the learner with contradictory patterns for the same first move.
replacement: Let a nearby staff member know you are engaging, then approach calmly — without blocking his exit or yours — introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter where staff can still see us, or is there something I can get you?'
basis: Project BETA de-escalation (Richmond et al. 2012) pairs verbal de-escalation with environmental and personal safety — adequate staff nearby, exit awareness, no isolated spaces; internal consistency with the keyed teaching of qb_saf_011 in this same bank.

quote: Thiamine before glucose — every time, before any IV dextrose in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient.
problem: In the stems this pearl summarizes, glucose is never emergently needed (fingerstick low-normal, routine D5W), so the keyed answers are safe in context — but the pearl hardens the rule into 'every time, before any IV dextrose.' The management is counterintuitive and residents get it wrong in the same direction the day-1 team did: buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal is generally treated by giving *more* buprenorphine, promptly and in substantially larger increments, to complete the transition to buprenorphine occupancy, alongside aggressive symptomatic treatment — not by stopping the drug. A resident who learns only that the reassurance was wrong will still stop the buprenorphine, which is precisely how this patient lost her MOUD.
replacement: telling a patient in precipitated withdrawal that this is "the medicine working" is both inaccurate and, predictably, treatment-ending — and the team also needs to know what to do instead, because the correct move is counterintuitive: precipitated withdrawal is generally treated by *continuing and rapidly escalating* buprenorphine to carry the patient through to full buprenorphine occupancy, not by stopping it, together with aggressive symptomatic treatment (antiemetic, alpha-2 agonist, non-opioid analgesia) and full-agonist analgesia where pain requires it

quote: Operationally (framed generally, never specifically): collaboratively engage the patient — and, with consent, a trusted other — to **reduce or remove access to lethal means at home** during the high-risk period

Effective counselling is means-specific and, in the US, largely firearm-specific: ask what is in the home, then negotiate temporary off-site storage with a trusted person, locking devices, and separating ammunition, plus securing medication supply. A resident told to operationalise this "never specifically" will produce a generic "make the home safe" line that neither changes access nor matches the intervention the page has just called the best-supported strategy in the field. For a Resident audience that carries med-legal accountability for this conversation, it is too thin.

In the US that means firearms first (temporary off-site storage with a trusted person, locking devices, ammunition stored separately) and then medication supply (quantity dispensed, lock box). Naming the specific means is what makes the counselling effective; naming methods is neither required nor what this is

quote: **Add phenobarbital** per institutional protocol, with an explicit preference for a **loading/replacement strategy rather than open-ended stacking**, given the ventilation and aspiration signal in the adjunct literature [3,9,10]. Airway monitoring is mandatory.

Without that, a resident re-doses on benzodiazepine intuitions, does not anticipate cumulative or delayed sedation on day 2–3, and may run a benzodiazepine taper on top of a phenobarbital load — which is the mechanism behind the ventilation and aspiration signal this very sentence cites.

The pharmacokinetics are why that distinction is real: phenobarbital's half-life is roughly 80–120 hours, so a load provides its own taper over several days, cannot be titrated back once given, and adds to any benzodiazepine still on board — decide the total load up front and stop the parallel benzodiazepine rather than running both. quote: Plan explicitly for **delivery**, when clearance abruptly normalizes and the risk direction reverses toward toxicity; hydration status during labor matters.
problem: The bullet names the physiology and stops before the management, inside a list the page titles "Practical monitoring changes in pregnancy" and inside a question the facilitator notes rank as one of three priorities. What a resident must actually decide is whether to continue, reduce, or withhold lithium around labour; that a level should be checked at delivery and in the early postpartum; and that the dose returns to the pre-pregnancy dose rather than the higher pregnancy dose once GFR falls — the single most common route to postpartum lithium toxicity. Lactation is omitted entirely, and it is the next question this patient will ask; residents commonly believe lithium is an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding, which is not current practice.
replacement: Plan explicitly for **delivery**, when clearance abruptly normalizes and the risk direction reverses toward toxicity. Decide in advance with obstetrics whether to continue lithium with close level monitoring and assured hydration or to reduce/withhold around labour (practice genuinely varies; reducing toward the pre-pregnancy dose in the 24–48 h before a planned delivery is one common approach). Check a level at delivery and in the early postpartum, and return to the **pre-pregnancy** dose rather than the higher pregnancy dose once GFR falls — this is the commonest route to postpartum toxicity. Counsel on transient neonatal effects (hypotonia, poor feeding), and address **breastfeeding** explicitly: lithium is not an absolute contraindication in a healthy term infant, but it requires a shared decision, infant monitoring, and a plan for infant hydration and levels during illness.
basis: Peripartum lithium management as described in perinatal-psychiatry guidance (NICE CG192 antenatal and postnatal mental health; the Bergink/Wesseloo peripartum lithium literature) and the standard postpartum dose-reversion point given the abrupt fall in GFR at delivery; current lactation guidance treats lithium as usable with infant monitoring rather than contraindicated. Whether to hold or continue at labour varies by centre, so the fix is to state the decision and its options, not to prescribe one.

quote: *anticholinergic* → supportive, remove agent, benzodiazepine ± physostigmine in select cases

quote: NMS typically resolves over **days to ~2 weeks** with agent withdrawal and supportive care — slower than SS, which usually clears in 24–72 h [1][4][5].
problem: 'Clears in 24–72 h' holds for short-half-life serotonergic agents and is false for the one this patient is actually taking. Fluoxetine's active metabolite norfluoxetine has a half-life of days to weeks, so fluoxetine-associated serotonin toxicity can be both delayed in onset and prolonged well past 72 hours — which also weakens the tempo argument the case uses to exclude SS. A resident could stop fluoxetine, expect resolution by day three, read persisting abnormality as evidence for a competing diagnosis, or clear the patient for a subsequent serotonergic agent or an MAOI far too early.
replacement: NMS typically resolves over **days to ~2 weeks** with agent withdrawal and supportive care — usually slower than serotonin toxicity, which clears within 24–72 h **for short-half-life agents. With fluoxetine (norfluoxetine half-life of days to weeks) or an MAOI, both onset and resolution can be substantially delayed, and a 5-week washout is required before starting an MAOI** [1][4][5].
basis: Fluoxetine elimination half-life 1–4 days and norfluoxetine 4–16 days (US prescribing information), hence the standard 5-week fluoxetine-to-MAOI washout; Boyer & Shannon, NEJM 2005 (this page's reference [1]) describes resolution within about 24 hours for short-acting serotonergic agents specifically.

quote: Note that HIPAA permits sharing for treatment, payment, and operations.
problem: On a confidentiality page for residents on an adult inpatient unit, HIPAA's treatment/payment/operations permission is stated without the exception that actually catches people: records from a federally assisted substance use disorder treatment program fall under 42 CFR Part 2, which is stricter than HIPAA and governs a large share of the co-occurring patients on the unit. A resident who takes "treatment, payment, and operations" as the whole rule will repeat SUD treatment information to an outside provider or a family member without the consent Part 2 requires — the most common confidentiality error made by trainees on an inpatient unit, and one with regulatory consequences the page never signals.
replacement: Note that HIPAA permits sharing for treatment, payment, and operations — but two carve-outs matter on an inpatient unit: **42 CFR Part 2** governs records originating from a federally assisted substance use disorder treatment program and has its own consent requirements (recent rulemaking aligns it more closely with HIPAA, so verify the current rule and whether your program is a Part 2 program), and psychotherapy notes are separately protected. Assume SUD-treatment information needs its own consent before you repeat it.
basis: 42 CFR Part 2 confidentiality of substance use disorder patient records; the 2024 Part 2 final rule aligns consent for treatment/payment/operations more closely with HIPAA — confirm the current rule text and local applicability, which is what would settle the exact wording here.

quote: Least-restrictive escalation: environment/1:1 sitter → verbal de-escalation → single lowest-effective enteral/IM agent → physical restraints only as time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation.
problem: The question asks residents to design the restraint-minimisation and monitoring plan, and the answer stops at 'time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation.' Residents are the ones who write and defend these orders. Nothing here says what 'time-limited' means for restraint used for violent or self-destructive behaviour — the one-hour in-person evaluation, the four-hour maximum order duration for adults, and the prohibition on PRN or standing restraint orders. That is the part of restraint practice this audience actually owns and is accountable for, and it is exactly what separates the resident-level answer from the student-level one.
replacement: Least-restrictive escalation: environment/1:1 sitter → verbal de-escalation → single lowest-effective enteral/IM agent → physical restraints only as time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation. For restraint or seclusion used for violent or self-destructive behaviour, know the regulatory floor you are signing to: an in-person evaluation by a physician/LIP or trained RN **within 1 hour** of initiation, an order duration capped at **4 hours** for adults 18 and over and renewable only after re-evaluation, **no PRN or standing restraint orders**, and monitoring documented at defined intervals until release.
basis: CMS Conditions of Participation, 42 CFR §482.13(e) (patients' rights: restraint and seclusion) and the aligned Joint Commission standards — the operative requirements for adult inpatient and ED restraint in US hospitals.
